sentences.text: They came back the next afternoon and did the second wall — the one that ran down the slope toward the small stony beach.
It was, Bríd said, the wall her mother had loved more.
"She always liked to walk down to the sea.
She said, if I am buried inland, my ghost will come here anyway.
So they buried her inland, in the churchyard, but I have always thought she comes here." Bríd said this as they walked, and Aisling could not tell if she was joking.
Bríd's face did not always tell.
The wall was six hundred stones long.
Aisling started at the top, near the crest of the slope.
Bríd walked more slowly, starting at the bottom, near the beach.
They worked toward each other.
Aisling looked at every stone.
Aisling found it about a third of the way down.
It was small, and it was low — at her knee, not her shoulder, so she almost missed it.
She was crouched to look at another stone when her eye caught it just below.
A small stone about the size of her two fists, plain, grey.
But scratched on the top of it, so faint that she had to tilt her head, was a small spiral — a coil turning inward, done with the point of a knife, a long time ago.
She called Bríd.
Bríd came slowly down the wall.
When she saw the stone, and the spiral, she stopped walking.
She did not say anything for a long time.
Then she said, very quietly, "Yes.
That's hers."
"How do you know?" Aisling asked.
Bríd said, "Because of the height.
My mother said, once, when I was small — if I ever leave a stone, it will be low.
So a child can read it.
She said that as a joke, one day, when we were sorting laundry, and I never forgot.
I thought she was joking.
But she wasn't." Bríd bent down slowly.
She put her hand flat against the stone.
"Sixty years," she said, more to the stone than to Aisling.
Then she said, "Help me lift it."
The stone came out of the wall with a soft grinding sound.
Behind it, in the dark hollow between it and the next layer of stones, was a small piece of folded paper.
It was old — very old — brown at the edges and dry as a wasp's nest.
Bríd took it out carefully.
She held it in her open palm.
It was smaller than Aisling's hand.
Bríd unfolded it slowly.
The paper cracked at the corners but held.
Inside, in careful old-fashioned pencil, in the old Aran Irish, were four lines.
Bríd read them silently.
Then she read them again.
Then she translated for Aisling, softly, because Aisling did not have that Irish.
She said: Bríd, daughter of mine, who will stay.
May the sea sing to you.
May the stone keep you.
May you have lived well by the time you read this.
Peig.
June, nineteen sixty-six.
Bríd was crying, quietly, without any sound.
Aisling had never seen her aunt cry.
She did not know what to do.
She sat very still beside her, on the grass by the wall, and after a moment she reached out and put her small hand on Bríd's arm.
After a while Bríd folded the paper again, carefully, and put it back into the hollow.
She lifted the stone and set it back in place.
It fitted exactly.
When it was in, you could not tell it had ever been moved.
The spiral was on top, small, hardly visible unless you knew.
"Why did you put it back?" Aisling asked.
Bríd said, "Because that is where she put it.
It is not for me to take home.
I have read it now.
That was what she wanted.
She wanted me to have read it, one day, in my own time, when I was ready.
Now I have.
It can go back to the wall.
Maybe someone else will find it a hundred years from now.
Maybe not.
That is not up to me."
They walked slowly back up to the cottage.
Bríd was quiet most of the way.
Just before they got to the door, she stopped, and she said to Aisling, "Thank you for coming this summer.
I would never have gone to look on my own.
I told myself, sixty years, that I would go one day.
I would never have gone.
I needed a child here with me.
That is what she knew.
That is what she meant by, you will know when you want to look."
Aisling said, "Will you leave one?
A stone, someday?" Bríd thought about it.
She said, "I don't know.
Maybe.
Maybe I will.
If I do, it will be for you.
If you come back to look for it, one day, when you are older, you will find it in that same wall.
Near the sea.
Low.
Where a child could read it." And she opened the cottage door, and they went in, and she put the kettle on for tea, and outside the small window the sea kept doing what it had always done.
